entries.root_cause: Authenticating commit-status evidence only by the shared github-actions[bot] creator and by pointing at a successful canonical workflow run was insufficient: any repository workflow with status-write authority can publish under the same bot identity and can point a forged status at a legitimate run for a different PR, command mode, or coordinate set. The status therefore was not yet bound to the actual trusted publisher job that produced it.

The live readiness verifier revalidated current head/base SHAs and mutable labels but treated any non-empty current head ref as acceptable. A branch rename can preserve the exact candidate commit while invalidating the canonical G1 branch-prefix classification, so SHA-only readiness left non-SHA implementation identity mutable after attestation.

The issue_comment workflow initially accepted github.event.repository.default_branch as the authoritative branch name. That event field is a creation-time snapshot, so a repository default-branch change during execution could leave resolve, final publication, and later readiness validating against a branch that was no longer the repository's current default branch.

The strict learning layer executed the delegated readiness falsifier under a permissive verifier but did not prove that the ledger-credited authorization probe still delegated to that falsifier. Removing the delegation therefore allowed the credited outer probe to remain green even while the readiness validator was weakened, breaking the semantic chain between ledger credit and the executable readiness guardrail.

A syntactically correct outer-to-inner readiness delegation was still insufficient because the imported alias could be rebound at runtime before the matching call. Static AST binding plus separate execution of the inner readiness probe did not prove that the ledger-credited outer probe actually invoked the intended delegated guardrail at runtime.

The runtime delegation proof authenticated only a public exception message. An unrelated pre-delegation helper could raise the same RuntimeError text and satisfy the check without invoking the injected readiness sentinel, so textual exception equality did not establish callback provenance.

The permissive-readiness sabotage accepted any AssertionError from the credited inner probe. A probe could detect the injected permissive verifier and raise immediately, preserving green strict validation without executing the negative readiness cases that were supposed to prove semantic liveness.

Even unique exception identity was insufficient while the delegation sentinel state spanned module import and credited-probe invocation. Candidate test code could call and catch the injected sentinel during import, retain that exception object, suppress the real delegated call later, and replay the captured exception while the accumulated call counter still appeared valid.

The strict readiness semantic proof still trusted candidate-controlled fragment labels and call counts rather than authenticating the actual readiness arguments. A weakened probe could label arbitrary permissive-verifier calls with the expected fragments while omitting every canonical fixture mutation, so syntactic case names did not prove the intended negative semantics were exercised.
